extracted.intended_audience: readers and members of polite society seeking guidance on gentlemanly conduct and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on what constitutes a 'gentleman' and the manners, dispositions, and social practices that form cultivated society; aimed at those who wish to behave with grace, authority, and social effectiveness. Emphasizes character, taste, and social utility rather than mere fashion or wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman as man of truth and self-mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman is 'a man of truth, lord of his own actions,' not dependent or servile to persons, opinions, or possessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express this lordship in behaviour; do not dodge or evade — 'a gentleman never dodges; his eyes look straight forward.' Truth and directness are foundational to courtesy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature (benevolence) as core of courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond force and truth, the gentleman's name denotes good-nature or benevolence: 'manhood first, and then gentleness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generosity ranges from small willingness to oblige up to magnanimity; social favorites are 'contented and contenting' and fill occasions appropriately. Examples: Fox's conduct toward a creditor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal force and original energy
rubrics_metrics.description: A leading quality is original energy — physical spirits and vigor that enable leadership in war, politics, or trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'animal' vigour lends the sense of power that makes difficult things easy; society's leaders must be 'up to the work of the world' and versatile in office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide social affinity and conversational range
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman has a 'wide affinity' that transcends clique and caste and makes him intelligible to many classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He should be 'good company for pirates and good with academicians' — able to converse and fraternize across social boundaries so that even truckmen and patricians can meet him on equal terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune as helpful but not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth is commonly regarded necessary for the man of the world, but Emerson insists money is not essential — personal force naturally leads to dispensation of worldly goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical exemplars (Diogenes, Socrates) show poverty is compatible with gentlemanly rank; fortune may aid appearance but does not define the gentleman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners as instruments to facilitate fellowship
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners aim to 'get rid of impediments' and facilitate life and conversation—like a railway that removes avoidable obstructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good forms remove obstacles to social energizing; manners that assist fellowship are 'good'; those that hinder (eg. quarrelsome, solitary behavior) are disliked by society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion as symbolic, fallible, but functional
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion is an equivocal semblance — often frivolous — but it rests on reality and functions to exclude pretenders and perpetuate cultivated manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both fashion's defects and uses: it organizes 'beauty of behavior' and is a 'hall of the Past,' admitting those who embody cultivated qualities while dismissing pretenders to 'Coventry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Composure and self-content (self-reliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society excuses many faults if a person exhibits composure and full self-satisfaction; self-reliance is highly valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the same attitude of mind in new companies; strong will is always in fashion. Avoid visible giddiness or being overwhelmed by new circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference, stateliness, and preservation of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer stately deference over excessive familiarity; maintain the 'island of a man' inviolate — preserve strangeness even with intimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each meeting as from 'foreign countries'; lovers should 'guard their strangeness.' Avoid too much mutual accommodation of trivial needs (don't anticipate someone's plate, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the primary point of courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: The first point of courtesy is truth; good-breeding's forms are grounded in truth rather than dissimulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid skulking or hiding behind etiquette; being true and direct underlies all polite forms. Examples: Napoleon's masking of expression criticized; truth recommended instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery and genuine hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: A good household needs a master who receives guests personally rather than hiding behind screens of luxury and ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Host should welcome and stand by guests (old feudal point that a gentleman should wait at his door for a sovereign); screens (luxuries) risk shielding the host from direct human encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception, taste, and homage to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders of men require intellectual perception and a reverence for beauty; manners include an intellectual quality — 'a homage to beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Love of beauty equates to love of measure/proportion; social success depends on quick but tempered perceptions and a cultivated taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and tempering of intellectual exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy and quick perception are needed but must be tempered; do not bring business omniscience into the palace of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may be 'too punctual and too precise' in society. Leave the pedantry and excessive exactness at the door; prefer gentle, measured discourse and avoid superlatives and shrillness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-natured sympathy and social heartiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The secret of social success is sympathy and heartiness — ability to 'fill the hour and the company' without uncomfortable egotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social favorites find fitting words for occasions across types of events (marriage, funeral, ball, jury); they enable fellowship rather than obstruct it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pretension and valuing genuine merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion and social circles naturally exclude pretenders; genuine merit and reality are what fashion secretly honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake ceremonious polish for substance; beware the 'false gentleman' who civility can sometimes disguise. True service and living kindness distinguish the real gentleman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of forms as protective but not dehumanizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Good forms of politeness are a science of defence to parry and intimidate, but they should not become mere fencing that hides reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When matched by equal skill, manners should drop their point and allow transparent fellowship; forms are useful but must be subordinate to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate convivial breadth (wit, intellectual splendor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine society values wit and the direct splendor of intellectual power as costly additions to its rule and credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellect should be present but shaded — the 'dry light' must shine but be tempered. Sleepy languid manners that conceal strength are often preferred in company to dazzling intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public deeds and moral actions as sources of aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic dispositions and public-spirited acts (rescuing, planting trees, aiding slaves) are the true centres of society and creators of fashion's highest ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: rescuing a drowning man, philanthropy, support of oppressed peoples; these moral acts generate genuine social leadership beyond mere polished manners.
